abstract: |
  Most faults of the Juan de Fuca plate system lie offshore, where earthquakes have been too poorly located
  to map them in three dimensions. We built a catalog of 172,340 earthquakes (2010–2016) from ocean-bottom
  and land seismometers with ensemble deep-learning phase picking, graph-network association and location,
  and calibrated local magnitudes. Planar alignments of the events define 141 rectangular fault surfaces
  that hold 70% of the located earthquakes, with uncertainties at every point. They resolve parallel and
  stepping strands of the Blanco transform, the Gorda Ridge segments, the Mendocino transform at depth and
  structures with no published counterpart. Nearest-neighbor clustering shows that how faults slip follows
  the tectonic setting: swarms dominate ridges and transforms, short productive sequences the triple
  junction, and isolated events the forearc. [TO UPDATE after the 3D relocation; ≤150 words.]

# Introduction

The Juan de Fuca, Gorda and Explorer plates are young, small and deforming. Their boundaries include
spreading ridges (Juan de Fuca, Gorda), long transforms (Blanco, Mendocino, Sovanco), a triple junction,
and the Cascadia subduction zone, all within 1,000 km. Most of these faults are offshore. Land networks
locate offshore earthquakes with errors of 10–20 km, so the published picture of offshore faults comes
from bathymetry, a few ocean-bottom deployments of months to a year on single segments, and
teleseismic relocations [@Braunmiller2008; @Ren2023; @Lange2026]. The community fault model of the
region contains no fault geometry built from earthquake locations, and no Blanco, Gorda or ridge faults
at all [@Hatem2021 and the CRESCENT Community Fault Model; Text S4].

The Cascadia Initiative deployed ocean-bottom seismometers across the whole plate from 2011 to 2015,
moving them each year. Combined with land stations, this array recorded the ridges, transforms, the
triple junction, the forearc and the volcanic arc at the same time. Machine-learning phase pickers now
work on ocean-bottom data [@Yuan2023; @Bornstein2023; @Niksejel2024], and graph neural networks
associate and locate the picks of large, changing networks [@McBrearty2023; @McBrearty2025].

We use this to ask three questions that need one consistent catalog across a whole plate system.
(1) Which faults are seismically active, and what is their three-dimensional architecture, offshore as
well as onshore? (2) How does the way faults slip — in isolated events, mainshock–aftershock sequences
or swarms — change between ridges, transforms, the triple junction, the forearc and the arc? (3) What
does a short, moving array reveal that permanent networks miss? Because the array moved every year, we
focus on spatial structure and on processes lasting hours to months, not on multi-year rate changes.

# Results

## A plate-wide catalog from a moving amphibious array

The catalog has 172,340 events from 2010 to 2016, located with 2,503,189 P and S picks on 696 stations,
322 of them on the seafloor (Fig. 1; Materials and Methods). Local magnitudes calibrated to ComCat exist
for 130,767 events (3,416 common events, scatter 0.21 magnitude units). The magnitude of completeness
(Mc) varies by a factor of 50 in energy across the region and through time, because the array moved:
[TO ADD from the Mc maps: Mc ranges by region and period, three methods; Fig. 2]. Epicenters are
reliable enough to place offshore earthquakes on bathymetric features: on the Gorda Ridge, catalog
epicenters fall on the axial valley, while ComCat epicenters of the same events lie 10–20 km east
(Text S5). Absolute depths are not yet reliable: 23.5% of events plot above the seafloor or ground in the
current locations, and a relocation in a 3D velocity model is under way [TO UPDATE].

## Seventy percent of earthquakes lie on 141 rectangular faults

We searched the catalog for planes rather than for dense clusters (Materials and Methods). A plane's
thickness tolerance follows the expected location error along its normal; planes grow along the plane
through connected events; every event then joins the plane that best contains it. Each fault is a
rectangle in its own plane, whether or not it reaches the surface, with an uncertainty normal to the
surface at every point (median 0.44 km), strike and dip intervals, and a stability score from repeated
runs (Text S1–S2).

The search returns 141 faults holding 53,291 of the 76,281 well-recorded events (70%; Fig. 3). The share
is highest where seismicity is concentrated on plate boundaries: 90% on the Blanco transform, 72% at the
Mendocino triple junction, 61% in the Puget Lowland, 50% in the Gorda plate. It is lowest in the sparse
forearc offshore Washington and Oregon (19–21%), where few planes reach 30 events. Six quarry-blast
clusters and four artefacts were removed after checks (Text S3). Axial Seamount, where cabled-array
catalogs already map the ring faults [@Wilcock2016; @Waldhauser2020], was left out.

We compared every fault with the published faults, ridge and transform segments and seismic zones of its
region (Text S4; Table S4). 94 match a known structure, 26 of them with high confidence, 17 duplicate a
neighbor, 10 are layers of seismicity rather than single faults, and 20 have no published counterpart.
Every fault carries at least one verified reference. Examples of strong matches: the Blanco Ridge
transform (strike within 2°), the north–south normal faults of the Cascadia Depression, the Escanaba
Trough and the Jackson and Central segments of the Gorda Ridge, the faults of the 2010 Mw 6.5 and 2014
Mw 6.8 Gorda earthquakes (strikes within 4–10° of the moment-tensor planes), the Garberville
low-frequency earthquake band that continues the Mendocino transform under land [@Shelly2025;
@Shelly2026], the Mount St. Helens seismic zone, the Twin Lakes segment of the Mount Hood fault zone,
and the fault of the 2014 Mw 6.4 Nootka sequence [@Hutchinson2023].

## The Blanco transform is a set of parallel and stepping strands

On the Blanco transform, single planes fitted across the whole zone cut across right-stepping strands.
We split the Blanco faults into strands found in map view, where locations are good, and kept two
overlapping parallel strands apart only when their separation is justified: the across-strike
distributions must be bimodal (Ashman's D > 2) [@Ashman1994] over their overlap and again within every
year, which rules out a shift between ocean-bottom deployments (Materials and Methods; Fig. 4). Twenty
strands remain; the 22 overlapping parallel pairs are 1.6–10.7 km apart (D = 2.8–15.9, minimum per
year 2.7). For most pairs a single dipping fault would need a dip of 3–48° to produce the offset, far from
the near-vertical strike-slip faults of the Blanco [@Braunmiller2008], so the separation is horizontal.

The strands reproduce what ocean-bottom studies resolved on single segments and connect them. The two
wall strands of the Surveyor Depression (5.3 km apart) match the strands about 7 km apart of
@Ren2023 and @Lange2026. The West Blanco–Surveyor and Blanco Ridge–Gorda Transform overlaps sit at the
pull-apart step-overs mapped from bathymetry [@Embley1992; @Braunmiller2008]. Two "deeper band" strands
2 km south of the Blanco Ridge and Gorda Transform were merged into their main strand: their offset
follows depth, as expected from depth-dependent location error, and the ocean-bottom catalogs see one
zone within 1.5 km [@Lange2026; @Kuna2019]. Pairs about 2 km apart at equal depth in the West Blanco
Depression and on the north wall of the Gorda Depression are finer than any published spacing; they are
candidates for new structure to be confirmed with the relocated catalog.

## How faults slip follows the tectonic setting

We classified events into background earthquakes, mainshock–aftershock sequences, swarms and
multiplets with the nearest-neighbor method in space, time and magnitude [@Baiesi2004; @Zaliapin2008;
@Zaliapin2013a; @Zaliapin2013] (Materials and Methods). The distribution of rescaled time and distance is
bimodal in every region, and the clustered mode disappears when event times are shuffled (Text S6). All
six large earthquakes of the period come out as mainshock–aftershock sequences with the mainshock first,
and the 2015 Axial eruption as one 632-event swarm.

Clustering follows the tectonic setting (Fig. 5). The ridges and transforms (Axial, Blanco, Gorda) are
about half background, and two thirds of their families of five or more events are swarms, with long,
chain-like trees. The Mendocino triple junction has fewer swarms (31%) and short, bushy sequences; 76% of
its events 1–2 magnitude units above Mc have no linked aftershock above Mc, consistent with
@Hsu2026. The forearc, Puget Lowland and onshore regions are 68–84% background. This is the dependence
on crustal temperature found in southern California and globally [@Zaliapin2013; @Zaliapin2016], here
across one plate system recorded by one array.

On the Blanco transform, swarms are short (median 4 hours) and compact (4 km), and the largest events
occur in swarms or doublets: the 2012 Mw 5.8 and 6.0 events share one swarm, and three M 5.4–5.9 events
struck within 13 hours in June 2015. Swarm shares are highest on the West Blanco, Surveyor and Cascadia
Depression strands (33–45% of events above Mc), in the pull-apart basins. Low aftershock productivity
and swarm-like sequences are typical of oceanic transforms, where aseismic slip loads small seismic
patches [@McGuire2005; @Roland2009; @Boettcher2009; @Kuna2019].

## Short-lived processes caught by the moving array

[TO WRITE with Fig. 6.] Candidates, each with its evidence so far:
(i) at Axial, swarm families rise from 1 per month in November 2014 to 16 in March 2015 before the April
2015 eruption, in a catalog independent of the cabled array [@Wilcock2016];
(ii) on the Gorda Ridge, a May 2013 swarm in the northern Escanaba Trough migrates at about 10 km/day,
a dike-like rate;
(iii) in the Gorda plate near 41.85°N, 126.1°W, a WNW-striking right-lateral source with repeated
M 4–5.7 events and no named fault;
(iv) a swarm off Brookings, Oregon, in August–November 2012 with no published counterpart;
(v) the Mendocino transform segment that ruptured in the 2016 Mw 6.6 earthquake was active in 2015,
before it.

# Discussion

[TO WRITE.] Points to develop:

1. **A seismicity-based fault model for the offshore plate boundaries.** None of the 3D faults in the
   community model comes from hypocenters; ours are the first for the Blanco, Gorda and Mendocino
   offshore faults, with uncertainties, and they can be versioned as locations improve
   [@Alongi2025; @Wang2013; @Ouillon2008].
2. **Transform architecture.** Parallel strands and overlapping step-overs along 350 km of the Blanco,
   with swarms concentrated in the pull-aparts, point to a transform still organizing
   [@Ren2023 call it immature]. The finest pairs (about 2 km) need the relocation.
3. **Thermal control of seismic behavior at plate scale.** Swarm-dominated ridges and transforms versus
   productive sequences at the triple junction and isolated forearc events, in one catalog.
4. **What a moving array can and cannot do.** Spatial structure and processes of hours to months, yes;
   rates over years, no. Completeness maps (Fig. 2) bound every comparison.
5. **Limits.** Absolute depths and dips await the 3D relocation; the per-region Mc keeps 27,555 events
   for clustering, so microswarms at the volcanoes are below it; focal mechanisms from our picks will test
   the fault surfaces.

# Materials and Methods

## Data and catalog

Continuous data from 728 land and ocean-bottom stations, 40–50°N and 131–122°W, 2010–2016, including
the Cascadia Initiative ocean-bottom array, were picked with an ensemble of EQTransformer models
[@Mousavi2020; @Yuan2023] in SeisBench [@Woollam2022]. Picks were associated with GENIE
[@McBrearty2023] and located with a graph-network double-difference method [@McBrearty2025] (catalog
v4, I. McBrearty). Pick completion, quality control and data issues are in Text S5. [TO UPDATE: 3D
relocation, NonLinLoc and GrowClust, catalog v5.]

## Magnitudes and completeness

Wood–Anderson amplitudes were measured for every pick in windows set by phase and distance, inverted for
event size, distance attenuation and station terms, and anchored to 3,416 ComCat local magnitudes;
moment magnitudes from regional moment tensors replace ML above 4.5 (Text S5). Mc was mapped on a 0.1°
grid from the nearest 250 events with three methods: maximum curvature with a +0.2 correction,
b-value stability, and goodness of fit [@Wiemer2000; @Cao2002; @Woessner2005], with bootstrap
uncertainty, for the whole period and for each deployment period [TO UPDATE with results].

## Fault surfaces

Events with at least four P and four S picks and non-negative depth were used. Planes were detected by
sequential local random sampling [@Fischler1981]: around seeds taken from dense to sparse, candidate
planes through the seed and two events within 10 km were scored by the number of free events within a
tolerance $\tau = 1.5\sqrt{(1.5\,|n_h|)^2 + (3\,n_z)^2}$ km, where $n$ is the unit normal (1.5 km
horizontal and 3 km vertical nominal relative errors). The best plane grew through events within $\tau$
that were connected in the plane (4 km cells), and was kept with at least 30 events, planarity
$\sqrt{\lambda_3/\lambda_2} \le 0.5$ and dip ≥ 30°. Events were then reassigned to the plane with the
smallest $|d|/\tau$ among planes whose rectangle contains them, and coplanar neighbors were merged. Each
fault is the rectangle spanning the 2–98% range of its events along strike and down dip, with a plane
or quadratic surface chosen by the Bayesian information criterion. Uncertainty normal to the surface
combines a bootstrap of the events, a Monte Carlo over location errors and the spread over model
choices; strike and dip intervals come from the bootstrap; stability is the overlap of each fault's
events across reruns with other random seeds and tolerances (Text S1–S2).

On the Blanco transform, strands were found in map view (lines within 20° of plate motion, 1.5 km half
width, grown along strike across gaps under 4 km). Two overlapping parallel strands were kept separate
only if Ashman's $D = \sqrt{2}\,|\mu_1-\mu_2|/\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$ of their across-strike
positions exceeds 2 over the overlap and within each year with at least 15 events in each [@Ashman1994].

Each fault was compared with the literature of its region; matches, confidence, evidence and verified
references are in Table S4.

## Clustering

For each event $j$ above Mc, the parent is the earlier event $i$ minimizing
$\eta_{ij} = t_{ij}\, r_{ij}^{d_f}\, 10^{-b m_i}$, with rescaled time $T = t\,10^{-q b m_i}$ and distance
$R = r^{d_f} 10^{-(1-q) b m_i}$, $q = 0.5$, $d_f = 1.6$, epicentral distance, and $b$ per region
[@Baiesi2004; @Zaliapin2008; @Zaliapin2013a]. The threshold $\eta_0$ comes from a two-component Gaussian
mixture on $\log_{10}\eta$ in each region. Links are limited to three rupture lengths [@Wells1994] or 10
km. Families are connected trees; within a family the largest event is the mainshock. A family of five or
more events is a swarm when at least two of three hold: largest minus second magnitude below 0.5; at
least 20% of events before the largest; mean leaf depth at least 2 with fewer than half of events
direct offspring of the largest [@Zaliapin2013; @Vidale2006]. Mc is the maximum curvature plus 0.2 per
region and year. Shuffled catalogs and variants of $d_f$, distance, Mc and threshold are in Text S6.
